definition.text: Harvesting a renewable resource, such as fish, forests, groundwater or wildlife, faster than it can replenish, to the point of diminishing returns.

facts.text: Ecologists count it among the five main activities threatening global biodiversity.
A population is overexploited when harvested at a rate its natural mortality and reproduction cannot sustain, which can wipe out populations or whole species.
Harvesting can be sustainable if it stays within limits, as in well-managed fisheries.
An aquifer is overexploited when water is extracted faster than it recharges; it is then said to be overdrafted.
Forests are overexploited when logging outpaces reforestation.
It threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates, and has affected about 40% of the bird species extinct since 1500.
Excluding edible fish, the illegal wildlife trade is valued at $10 billion a year.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons explains how people sharing a resource, each acting in self-interest, can overexploit and destroy it.

definition.text: The crash of a fished population, conventionally when its biomass falls by more than 95 percent of the highest level recorded.

facts.text: Pushing harvests past the maximum sustainable yield, usually reached near 30% of pre-harvest biomass, leads to collapse.
Atlantic cod collapsed abruptly in 1992 after heavy exploitation and failed to recover even after fishing stopped.
About 25% of world fisheries are overexploited below the biomass that maximizes sustainable yield.
A 2008 study found strong evidence that individual transferable quotas help prevent collapses and restore declining fisheries.

definition.text: Knock-on effects through a food web when overharvesting removes a key species, especially a top predator.

facts.text: Losing a top predator lets its prey multiply and overexploit their own food, sometimes until they too collapse.
Hunting of sea otters released sea urchins, which stripped kelp into urchin barrens and caused secondary extinctions.
After a 1911 treaty protected the last 32 sea otters in one group, they multiplied and the depleted areas slowly recovered.

definition.text: The two-way link in which clearing forests warms the climate and a changing climate in turn damages forests.

facts.text: Land use change, mainly deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels.
Emissions come from burning forest biomass and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon.
As of 2019 deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
The relationship is an amplifying feedback: more tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms and more tree loss.
Standing tropical forests help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C.
In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and forest ecosystem collapse.

title: Deforestation and rainfall
article: Deforestation and climate change#Changes in rainfall

definition.text: The drying effect of forest loss: fewer trees release less water vapour, so less rain falls nearby.

facts.text: Reduced rainfall brings a hotter, drier climate, longer dry seasons, more fires and disrupted pollination.
A 2025 study estimated deforestation caused about 74% of the decline in dry-season rainfall across the Brazilian Legal Amazon from 1985 to 2020.
Deforestation in the Congo is expected to cut regional rainfall by up to 8-10% by 2100.

definition.text: The change in how much sunlight a cleared landscape reflects, which alters warming beyond the effect of released carbon.

facts.text: Studies since the early 1990s show large-scale deforestation north of 50°N gives net global cooling, while tropical deforestation produces substantial warming.
Carbon-only metrics miss this because bare high-latitude ground is much more reflective than intact forest.

definition.text: How well represented a species is in a particular ecosystem, usually counted as individuals per sample.

facts.text: Relative species abundance compares one species' abundance with that of others in the ecosystem; both measures feed into biodiversity calculations.
Large animals are counted with methods such as spotlight, track and roadkill counts; plants are often measured by the share of a plot they cover.
In most ecosystems a few species are abundant and many are rare; abundant species tend to be generalists and rare ones specialists.
Abundant species produce more colonizing offspring, a feedback that yields widespread core species and scarce satellite species.

definition.text: A description of how common or rare each species is within an ecosystem.

facts.text: It is one of the most basic and widely used measurements in ecology, with many methods of analysis.
Distributions are usually skewed so that a few species make up most of the individuals collected.

definition.text: A quick field rating that scores a species in a plot as Dominant, Abundant, Frequent, Occasional or Rare.

facts.text: DAFOR and ACFOR are semi-quantitative ratings based on viewing an area of set size.
They give rough estimates but are not exact or objective, so better methods should be used where available.
